"People said it was impossible, but now it’s no longer optional."

According to [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/irans-capital-has-run-out-of-water-forcing-it-to-move/):

> Since at least 2008, scientists have warned that unchecked groundwater pumping for the city and for agriculture [was rapidly draining the country’s aquifers](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2008GL033814). The overuse did not just deplete underground reserves—it destroyed them, as the land compressed and sank irreversibly. One [recent study](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adk3039) found that Iran’s central plateau, where most of the country’s aquifers are located, is sinking by more than 35 centimeters each year. As a result, the aquifers lose about 1.7 billion cubic meters of water annually as the ground is permanently crushed, leaving no space for underground water storage to recover…. 

> This is not the first time Iran’s capital has moved. Over the centuries, it has shifted many times, from Tabriz to Isfahan to Shiraz. Some of these former capitals still thrive while others exist only as ruins…

Most experts cite the unprecedented severity and urgency of Tehran's water crisis as a strong driver increasing the probability: existential ecological threats, public warnings of city evacuation, and repeated statements by President Pezeshkian that relocating the capital is 'no longer optional' all signal that an announcement is more likely than in past years or comparable global cases. Multiple experts (Public Administration, Urban Planning, Political Science, Urban Studies, and Middle East Studies) note that the president has gone beyond generic rhetoric, referencing specific regions (Makran, Hormozgan) as candidate destinations, and that government councils are reportedly studying feasibility, which further raises the probability.

However, all experts emphasize significant barriers that temper the likelihood of a formal announcement meeting the strict resolution criteria. These include severe institutional inertia, bureaucratic risk aversion, elite factionalism, the need for consensus among powerful actors (especially the Supreme Leader and IRGC), vast logistical and financial costs (estimates exceeding $77 billion), and the fine print's requirement for a specific county- or city-level designation rather than vague intent. Historical and global base rates for such capital relocation announcements in times of crisis are very low, as most similar situations have seen delay or ambiguous promises rather than formal, location-specific policy shifts. Implementation skepticism, possible fears of backlash or regime destabilization, and uncertainty around elite cohesion are also mentioned frequently as factors decreasing the probability.

No experts assess the scenario as highly likely (>70%). The estimates span a range, with the lowest probability at 29% and the highest at 67%. The modal reasoning is that the probability is substantially higher than in ordinary times—due to the intensity of crisis and official rhetoric—but still more likely than not that Iran will fall short of making a formal, binding announcement specifying a new capital before the January 3, 2026 deadline. Some experts judge the chance just below even odds (e.g., 37%, 38%, 40%, 45%), while two assign moderately higher values (56%, 65%, 67%) on the basis of the exceptional moment and recent specific presidential statements. Across the board, experts agree that most likely, Iran will continue to amplify plans and proposals, but may ultimately defer a precise and official designation due to political and institutional constraints.

In summary, expert consensus holds that while Iran is facing systemic pressure that makes an official, specific capital relocation announcement far more plausible than would normally be expected, entrenched practical and political obstacles mean such an announcement remains less likely than not in the brief window before the question's deadline. Most estimates center between 30% and 55% probability, citing both the acute crisis and historical/political inertia.
